# The Problem {.center}

## Meet Ludwig

::: {.tag}
Rexburg, ID · 83440 · 9:40 PM
:::

::: {.chat}
::: {.chat-head}
<span>Summit Wireless · Support Chat</span> <span style="float:right">9:40 PM</span>
:::
::: {.chat-body}
::: {.bubble .me}
<span class="who">Ludwig</span>My internet has been out for 20 minutes. What's going on?
:::

::: {.bubble .them .fragment}
<span class="who">Summit Support Bot</span>Good news: there are **no known outages in your area!** Try unplugging your router for 30 seconds and plugging it back in. If that doesn't work, I can schedule a technician visit ($79).
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Read it in character. Pause after the bot reply: "Seems like a pretty good answer, right?"
:::

## What Ludwig did next

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .fragment}
[↻ Restarted the router]{.ct}

Three times.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[🧾 Booked the technician]{.ct}

Tomorrow, 8–10 AM. **$79.**
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[📱 Got a text]{.ct}

::: {.chat style="margin:0.3em 0 0; max-width:none"}
::: {.chat-body}
::: {.bubble .them style="max-width:100%"}
<span class="who">Neighbor</span>is your internet out too??
:::
:::
:::
:::
:::

## There *was* an outage

::: {.incident}
[Network Ops · Incident #4471]{.tag}

**83440 (Rexburg):** Fiber cut reported at **9:15 PM**

Crews on site. Estimated restore: **11:30 PM**

Reported **25 minutes** before Ludwig asked.
:::

::: {.big-q .fragment}
So why did the bot say there wasn't?
:::

# Discuss {.center}

## Why might that have happened?

With your partner, come up with **at least two** explanations.

::: {.incremental}
- Did the model make it up?
- Did the bot even have access to outage data?
- If it did, what could go wrong between the bot and that data?
:::

::: {.notes}
3 minutes. Collect answers on the board. Likely guesses: hallucination, stale data, no outage tool at all, wrong ZIP, API down. Don't confirm any yet. "Hold onto those; let's follow the code."
:::

::: {.why}
The bot answers Ludwig, but **every fact it needs lives in a system the chatbot team doesn't own**. Months ago, they hand-wrote a wrapper for each one.
:::

## The wrapper {auto-animate=true}

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1|2-3|4|5-7"}
# support_bot/wrappers.py · chatbot team · written in March
def check_outage(zip_code: str) -> str:
    """Check whether there is a known network outage in a ZIP code."""
    outages = network_ops_api.get("/outages", params={"zip": zip_code})
    if not outages:
        return "No known outages."
    return outages[0]["summary"]
```

::: {.why}
Totally reasonable code. It worked for six months. The chatbot team wrote it by reading Network Ops' API docs **as they were in March**.
:::

## Meanwhile, in another repo {auto-animate=true}

```{.java code-line-numbers="|3|4|5"}
// network-ops/OutageController.java · Network Ops team · shipped last week
@GetMapping("/outages")
public List<Outage> outages(
        @RequestParam(name = "postal_code", required = false) String postalCode) {  // was: "zip"
    return repo.findByPostalCode(postalCode);
}
```

::: {.why}
Network Ops renamed a parameter: `zip` → `postal_code`. Different team, different language, different release schedule. **Nobody told the chatbot team.** Why would they? It's *their* API.
:::

## Put them together

```{.python code-line-numbers="4|5-6"}
# support_bot/wrappers.py
def check_outage(zip_code: str) -> str:
    """Check whether there is a known network outage in a ZIP code."""
    outages = network_ops_api.get("/outages", params={"zip": zip_code})   # "zip" is ignored now
    if not outages:                                                       # postal_code=null -> []
        return "No known outages."
    return outages[0]["summary"]
```

::: {.why}
<span class="bad">No crash. No error. No hallucination.</span> The model did exactly what it should: it trusted its tool. The tool was wrong.
:::

::: {.notes}
Go back to the board. Whose guess was closest? "The model made it up" is the most common guess and it's wrong: the model behaved perfectly.
:::

::: {.why}
Summit now wants the same three systems in **three** AI apps. 3 apps × 3 systems = **9 wrappers**, all written and maintained by people who don't own the systems they wrap. Add a fourth system and it's 12.
:::

## The real problems

::: {.incremental}
1. **You don't own the code.** Another team, another language, another release schedule.
2. **Integrations drift and break silently.** A renamed field became a confident wrong answer.
3. **Every app × every system.** Wrappers multiply.
4. **The wrong people maintain them.** The team that knows the system isn't the team keeping the wrapper alive.
:::

# Brainstorm {.center}

## How would you make sure this never happens again?

With your partner, pick **one** idea and be ready to defend it.

- You can't control when Network Ops ships changes.
- Three apps (and counting) need the same three systems.
- Whatever you pick, someone has to maintain it. **Who?**

::: {.notes}
4 minutes. Expect: tests/monitoring on the wrapper, a shared company library, API versioning/contracts, "just tell us when you change it." All reasonable. Push on the "who maintains it?" question until someone says "the team that owns the system." That's the door into MCP.
:::

# The Smallest MCP Integration {.center}

## What if the owner shipped the tool?

::: {.why}
Same nine connections, but **no one writes them by hand.** The owners publish **3 servers**, once. Apps just plug in. When Network Ops renames a field, they update *their own* server.
:::

## Network Ops' side: a server {auto-animate=true}

::: {.tag}
network_ops/outage_server.py · owned by Network Ops
:::

```{.python}
from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Network Ops")
```

::: {.why}
**FastMCP** is the standard Python library for writing MCP servers. The name is what connecting apps see.
:::

## Network Ops' side: a server {auto-animate=true}

::: {.tag}
network_ops/outage_server.py · owned by Network Ops
:::

```{.python code-line-numbers="5"}
from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Network Ops")

OUTAGES = {"83440": "Fiber cut reported at 9:15 PM. Crews on site, ETA 11:30 PM."}
```

::: {.why}
A stand-in for their real monitoring database. The point: **the data lives with the people who own it.**
:::

## Network Ops' side: a server {auto-animate=true}

::: {.tag}
network_ops/outage_server.py · owned by Network Ops
:::

```{.python code-line-numbers="7-10"}
from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Network Ops")

OUTAGES = {"83440": "Fiber cut reported at 9:15 PM. Crews on site, ETA 11:30 PM."}

@mcp.tool
def check_outage(zip_code: str) -> str:
    """Check whether there is a known network outage in a ZIP code."""
    return OUTAGES.get(zip_code, "No known outages.")
```

::: {.why}
One decorator. The **function name, type hints, and docstring** become the tool's schema, just like `@tool` in LangChain.
:::

## Network Ops' side: a server {auto-animate=true}

::: {.tag}
network_ops/outage_server.py · owned by Network Ops
:::

```{.python code-line-numbers="12-13"}
from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Network Ops")

OUTAGES = {"83440": "Fiber cut reported at 9:15 PM. Crews on site, ETA 11:30 PM."}

@mcp.tool
def check_outage(zip_code: str) -> str:
    """Check whether there is a known network outage in a ZIP code."""
    return OUTAGES.get(zip_code, "No known outages.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()
```

::: {.why}
That's the whole server. **Thirteen lines**, and Network Ops owns every one of them.
:::

## Look familiar?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Your tool (Lesson 1-2)**

```{.python}
from langchain.tools import tool

@tool
def check_outage(zip_code: str) -> str:
    """Check for an outage in a ZIP code."""
    ...
```

Lives **in your agent's code**.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Their MCP tool**

```{.python}
from fastmcp import FastMCP
mcp = FastMCP("Network Ops")

@mcp.tool
def check_outage(zip_code: str) -> str:
    """Check for an outage in a ZIP code."""
    ...
```

Lives **in their server**, in a separate process.
:::
::::

::: {.why}
Same shape, different owner. That's most of MCP.
:::

```{.python code-line-numbers="10-12"}
from pathlib import Path
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.mcp import MCPAdapter

async with MCPAdapter(Path("outage_server.py")) as adapter:
    tools = await adapter.list_tools()

agent = create_agent("google_genai:gemini-flash-lite-latest", tools)

result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [
    {"role": "user", "content": "My internet in 83440 is out. What's going on?"}
]})
```

::: {.why}
`ainvoke`, not `invoke`: MCP tools talk over a connection, so they're **async-only**. `agent.invoke(...)` fails the moment the model picks an MCP tool.
:::

## Now Network Ops renames the field {auto-animate=true}

::: {.tag}
network_ops/outage_server.py · Network Ops ships an update
:::

```{.python code-line-numbers="8-10"}
from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Network Ops")

OUTAGES = {"83440": "Fiber cut reported at 9:15 PM. Crews on site, ETA 11:30 PM."}

@mcp.tool
def check_outage(postal_code: str) -> str:
    """Check whether there is a known network outage in a postal code."""
    return OUTAGES.get(postal_code, "No known outages.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()
```

::: {.why}
The exact change that broke Ludwig's bot. This time, Network Ops makes it **in their own server**.
:::

# How It Actually Works {.center}

## What "Model Context Protocol" means

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Model]{.ct}

For AI models. The thing reading the tool list is an LLM, so descriptions are written *for a model*.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[Context]{.ct}

Everything a model can use beyond its training: **tools** to call, **resources** to read, **prompts** to start from.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[Protocol]{.ct}

Agreed-on rules for the messages. Like HTTP for web pages: any browser, any website. Any MCP client, any MCP server.
:::
:::

::: {.why .fragment}
MCP standardizes **the connection**, not the tools. Network Ops decides what their tools do. MCP decides how everyone asks for them.
:::

::: {.why}
**Before step 1**, the client already asked the server "what tools do you have?" (`tools/list`). That's how the model knew `check_outage` existed. Two processes, **one protocol** in the middle. Neither side sees the other's code.
:::

## What goes over the wire

::: {.tag}
Your agent → Network Ops
:::

```{.json}
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list"}
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.tag}
Network Ops → your agent
:::

```{.json}
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": {"tools": [{
  "name": "check_outage",
  "description": "Check whether there is a known network outage in a postal code.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"postal_code": {"type": "string"}},
    "required": ["postal_code"]
  }}]}}
```
:::

::: {.why .fragment}
Step 0: **discovery.** This reply is where the model learned about `postal_code`. When Network Ops renamed it, this message changed, and your agent got the new name for free. (Real messages, trimmed.)
:::

## What goes over the wire (continued)

::: {.tag}
Your agent → Network Ops
:::

```{.json}
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call",
 "params": {"name": "check_outage", "arguments": {"postal_code": "83440"}}}
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.tag}
Network Ops → your agent
:::

```{.json}
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "result": {"content": [{
  "type": "text",
  "text": "Fiber cut reported at 9:15 PM. Crews on site, ETA 11:30 PM."}]}}
```
:::

::: {.why .fragment}
Steps 3 and 6: **the call.** Plain JSON. That's why the server can be written in any language: Python, Java, TypeScript, it doesn't matter. Anything that can read and write these messages can be an MCP server.
:::

## More than tools

::: {.cards}
::: {.card style="border-color:#7ee787"}
[🔧 Tools]{.ct}

Functions the model **calls**.

`check_outage(postal_code)`

*Most servers are mostly this. It's all we use today.*
:::

::: {.card style="border-color:#79c0ff"}
[📄 Resources]{.ct}

Data the app can **read**.

`outages://rexburg/map`

*Like a file the server shares.*
:::

::: {.card style="border-color:#d2a8ff"}
[💬 Prompts]{.ct}

Templates the **user** picks.

`/handle-outage-complaint`

*Network Ops' best script for outage calls.*
:::
:::

::: {.why}
The three **core server features** from the prep reading. One connection can carry all three.
:::

## Two ways to connect {.transports}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{=html}
<svg class="diagram" viewBox="0 0 400 190" role="img" aria-label="A spider web icon for stdio.">
  <g stroke="#ff7b72" stroke-width="2" fill="none" transform="translate(200,95)">
    <path d="M0,-85 L0,85 M-85,0 L85,0 M-60,-60 L60,60 M60,-60 L-60,60"/>

    <polygon points="0,-50 35,-35 50,0 35,35 0,50 -35,35 -50,0 -35,-35"/>
    <polygon points="0,-75 53,-53 75,0 53,53 0,75 -53,53 -75,0 -53,-53"/>
  </g>
</svg>
```

### stdio: Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man

- **Local.** Lives on your machine
- **Swoops in when needed.** The client launches the server, and it's gone when the client quits
- **One per client.** Other computers get their own (the Spider-Verse)
- **Found on GitHub** or a package: `python outage_server.py`, `uvx ...`, `npx ...`
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{=html}
<svg class="diagram" viewBox="0 0 400 190" role="img" aria-label="An arc reactor icon for HTTP.">
  <g transform="translate(200,95)">
    <circle r="80" fill="none" stroke="#79c0ff" stroke-width="2" opacity="0.5"/>
    <circle r="62" fill="none" stroke="#79c0ff" stroke-width="10" stroke-dasharray="18 9"/>
    <circle r="40" fill="#161b22" stroke="#79c0ff" stroke-width="3"/>
    <polygon points="0,-30 26,15 -26,15" fill="none" stroke="#79c0ff" stroke-width="3"/>
    <circle r="12" fill="#79c0ff"/>
  </g>
</svg>
```

### HTTP: Stark Industries

- **Remote.** Lives on a server somewhere else
- **Always on.** Already running before you connect
- **Serves many clients.** Spin up more Iron Man suits when traffic grows
- **Found on a company's website:** `https://docs.langchain.com/mcp`
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Hold on to these two: in the cloned repo, they'll run the same server both ways.
:::

## Same server, two transports

| | stdio (Spider-Man) | HTTP (Stark) |
|---|---|---|
| Server's last line | `mcp.run()` | `mcp.run(transport="http", port=8000)` |
| Who starts the server | **your agent**, as a subprocess | **the owner**, and it keeps running |
| Your agent's target | `Path("outage_server.py")` | `"http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp"` |
| Clients per server | one | many |
| Where it can live | your machine | anywhere with a URL |
| Everyday examples | filesystem, Blender, desktop apps | Slack, GitHub, LangChain docs |

::: {.why}
Only the **target** changes in your code. The tools, the agent, and the `ainvoke` stay the same.
:::

## Like USB

::: {.incremental}
- You plug in a mouse. You don't know how USB talks to it. **It just works.**
- The mouse maker didn't write a driver for *your* laptop. The laptop maker didn't write support for *their* mouse.
- Both followed **the standard**.
:::

. . .

::: {.why}
MCP is USB for AI tools: Network Ops builds the device (server), you build the laptop (agent), and **the protocol is the port**.
:::

## Run it both ways (20 min, pairs)

```{.bash code-line-numbers="|1-3|5-6|8-12"}
git clone https://github.com/byuidatascience/summit-wireless-mcp
cd summit-wireless-mcp
uv sync                      # then copy .env.example to .env and add your key

# 1. Spider-Man: one terminal. The agent launches the server itself.
uv run support_bot/agent.py

# 2. Stark: two terminals. Network Ops starts the server and leaves it running...
uv run fastmcp run network_ops/outage_server.py:mcp --transport http --port 8000

# ...and your agent only knows the URL.
uv run support_bot/agent.py --http
```

::: {.why}
In Stark mode, **watch terminal 1**: every `POST /mcp` line is your agent talking to Network Ops. Then stop the server and ask again. What happens?
:::

## Fix Ludwig's whole night

Ludwig also booked a **$79 visit** he doesn't need. FieldPro's server can find and cancel appointments.

Connect your agent to **both** servers by changing only its `target`:

```{.python code-line-numbers="|2|3"}
target = {"mcpServers": {
    "network": {"command": "python", "args": [str(NETWORK_OPS)]},
    "field":   {"command": "python", "args": [str(REPO / "field_service" / "scheduling_server.py")]},
}}
```

> *"Hi, it's Ludwig in 83440. My internet is out and I booked a technician for tomorrow. Do I still need them?"*

::: {.why}
Tool names get a prefix per server: `network_check_outage`, `field_cancel_appointment`. **Stretch:** be the billing team: write a server that gives Ludwig an outage credit, and connect it as a third.
:::

:::

## Add the LangChain docs to your agent {auto-animate=true .compact}

::: {.tag}
Your Project 1 agent · main.py
:::

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-7"}
import asyncio
from langchain.mcp import MCPAdapter

async def build_agent():
    async with MCPAdapter("https://docs.langchain.com/mcp") as adapter:
        docs_tools = await adapter.list_tools()
    return create_agent("google_genai:gemini-flash-lite-latest", docs_tools + my_tools)

def get_response(prompt: str) -> str:
    result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]})
    return result["messages"][-1].text
```

::: {.why}
A **URL** target: Stark Industries. LangChain runs this server; you just connect. `docs_tools + my_tools` mixes MCP tools with your own `@tool` functions.
:::

## Add the LangChain docs to your agent {auto-animate=true .compact}

::: {.tag}
Your Project 1 agent · main.py
:::

```{.python code-line-numbers="9-11"}
import asyncio
from langchain.mcp import MCPAdapter

async def build_agent():
    async with MCPAdapter("https://docs.langchain.com/mcp") as adapter:
        docs_tools = await adapter.list_tools()
    return create_agent("google_genai:gemini-flash-lite-latest", docs_tools + my_tools)

async def get_response(agent, prompt: str) -> str:
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]})
    return result["messages"][-1].text
```

::: {.why}
MCP tools are async-only, so `invoke` becomes **`await ... ainvoke`**, and the function becomes `async def`.
:::

## Add the LangChain docs to your agent {auto-animate=true .compact}

::: {.tag}
Your Project 1 agent · main.py
:::

```{.python code-line-numbers="13-21"}
import asyncio
from langchain.mcp import MCPAdapter

async def build_agent():
    async with MCPAdapter("https://docs.langchain.com/mcp") as adapter:
        docs_tools = await adapter.list_tools()
    return create_agent("google_genai:gemini-flash-lite-latest", docs_tools + my_tools)

async def get_response(agent, prompt: str) -> str:
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]})
    return result["messages"][-1].text

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent()
    while True:
        prompt = input("Input: ")
        if prompt == "exit": break
        print(await get_response(agent, prompt))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

::: {.why}
`main` becomes async too, and **`asyncio.run(main())`** starts it. A script has no event loop until you start one. (Colab already had one, which is why plain `await` worked there.)
:::

> *"How do I add short-term memory to a LangChain agent?"*

- Did it call `search_docs_by_lang_chain`? How can you tell?
- Your agent can now read docs **you didn't write, maintained by people you've never met**, and it'll stay current when they update them.
- ✅ That's the **"Connect to LangChain MCP"** requirement for Project 1.

## Keep plugging things in

```{.python}
target = {"mcpServers": {
    "docs":  {"url": "https://docs.langchain.com/mcp"},
    "fetch": {"command": "uvx", "args": ["mcp-server-fetch"]},
    # ...anything from the prep reading
}}
```

::: {.why}
Every server you connect counts toward the **most MCP servers connected** leaderboard. Before you connect one, ask: *who wrote this, and what can its tools change?*
:::
